newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Oil price slumps as market turns bearish.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Oil price slumps as market turns bearish.

text.p: Oil prices in New York slumped nearly $1 a barrel Thursday, as the turn from a bull to a bear market gathered pace.

Oil traders said news of an extended U.S.-brokered ceasefire between rival Kurdish factions, which may bring closer a deal to allow a limited lifting of sanctions on Iraqi oil exports, helped to spur the sell-off.
"The rationale is that with the (U.S.) election coming to end and the appearance of stability in Iraq, the way has been opened for an Iraqi oil-for-food deal," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.
But Thursday's action was an extension of a sell-off which has knocked more than 10 percent off crude oil futures prices in New York since they peaked at a post-Gulf War high last week.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), crude for December delivery ended off 93 cents at $23.35 barrel.

"We are moving to a new and lower trading range near term of between $21.50 and $24.00. This Kurdish ceasefire is suggesting to the market that the oil-for-food deal could be expedited," said Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch.

The deal, which was about to implemented two months ago but was suspended by the United Nations in late August when Baghdad intervened to aid one of the Kurdish factions, would allow sales of up to $2 billion of oil over six months to pay for humanitarian relief.
Though latching onto Thursday's progress in the Kurdish talks, the market's bearish turn also has followed a turn in the supply-demand situation in the U.S.

Crude prices ran up about 30 percent since the summer lows to last week's peak and heating oil surged by 50 percent over the same period as low stocks levels led to worries that a cold winter could result in shortages and higher prices.
Since peaking in early October, however, heating oil futures have slumped 14 percent since as it became clear that U.S. refiners had cranked up to record production levels to fill the inventory gap.

November heating oil futures, which expired on Thursday, fell more than two cents a gallon on the day to end at 66.34 cents a gallon, down from the post-Gulf War high of 76.75 cents seen on October 9.

The head of the American Petroleum Institute, Charles DiBona, said on Thursday that production of heating oil "has been reaching record levels." He said the worry about low stocks, which together with imports make up only five percent of supply, had been overdone.
Meanwhile, DiBona said that the refining industry, despite the period of high heating oil and diesel prices, were suffering from chronically low margins.
"It is extremely difficult to make money in refining," he said. "even at the best margins, a typical refinery hardly covers the cost of investment."

According to Salomon Brothers figures released earlier this week, integrated oil companies' refining and marketing margins so far in the fourth quarter are running at their lowest all year and more than 10 percent below the same period last year.
Among integrated oil companies' shares on Thursday, Exxon Corp was down 3/8 at $88 5/8 and Texaco Inc was down 1 3/8 at $101 5/8, while among the pure refiners Sun Co was down 1/2 at $22 3/8.
